questions.question: Explain how health and welfare affect development, with South African examples.
questions.expected_answer: Illness reduces work, schooling and investment and raises costs: malaria killed over 600 000 in 2022, about 95 per cent in Africa; HIV killed working-age adults and orphaned children (South Africa has about 7,8 million people with HIV and the largest treatment programme); TB remains a leading killer; stunting affects learning. Health also depends on water, sanitation, nutrition and vaccines. Welfare protects the poor: about 18-19 million grant recipients; school meals for about 9 million learners; brain drain weakens health systems.

questions.question: Explain why education, particularly of girls, is important for development, and why quality matters.
questions.expected_answer: Education raises skills, productivity and earnings (about 9-10 per cent per extra year), supports health and democracy and supplies professionals. Educated women marry later, have fewer and healthier children who attend school, earn incomes and gain a voice. Barriers: poverty, early marriage, chores, lack of toilets and sanitary products. Quality matters: PIRLS 2021 found about 81 per cent of South African Grade 4 learners could not read for meaning, linked to Bantu Education's legacy, overcrowding and poverty.

questions.question: Explain how political stability and governance affect development, using a contrasting example.
questions.expected_answer: Stability and good governance (rule of law, accountability, low corruption) allow investment and public services. Conflict destroys infrastructure, kills, displaces people and diverts spending (eastern DRC, South Sudan, Sudan), creating a conflict trap. Corruption diverts public money (South Africa's state capture, Zondo Commission 2018-2022). Botswana, very poor in 1966, found diamonds (1967), managed revenue through Debswana, held regular elections, kept corruption low and invested in services, becoming upper-middle-income.
